note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: Is the answer an integer or a string (leading zeros)?
Can fewer than three digits ever give a larger number?
Must the chosen digits be contiguous?
hints: Adding a digit to a chosen subsequence never makes the number smaller, so always pick exactly three.
The first chosen digit must leave two digits after it: take the largest digit among the first N - 2.
Take its leftmost occurrence so the later windows stay as wide as possible, then repeat for the second and third places.
invariants: each chosen digit leaves enough positions for the remaining places
taking the leftmost maximum never shrinks the later choices
tradeoffs: The greedy window scan is O(N * 3); a monotonic stack generalises to any length
hack2hire:6789754f11318cc872dd83ec.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: largest ordered three-digit pick

clarifyingQuestions: How is the hierarchy given, and which node is the root?
Are both employees guaranteed to be in the tree?
Can an employee be its own lowest common manager?
How deep can the hierarchy be?
hints: Record each employee's manager and depth in one pass from the root.
Lift the deeper of the two employees until both are at the same depth.
Then lift both one level at a time; the first common name is the answer.
invariants: after lifting, both pointers are at equal depth
the root is a common manager of every pair
chooseWhen: One-off queries on a deep tree without recursion
tradeoffs: Binary lifting answers many queries in O(log n) each at O(n log n) memory
hack2hire:67cb459e9db31a8671abf92c.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: lowest common manager in an n-ary org chart

constraints: every skeleton has word's length and uses [a-z-]
clarifyingQuestions: What is the second matching rule for dash positions?
Must a skeleton contain at least one dash?
Is the output in input order, and are duplicates kept?
hints: Non-dash positions are a direct comparison.
Under the dashes, only remember the first hidden letter.
Every later dash must hide that same letter.
invariants: all dashes seen so far hide one letter
every non-dash position seen so far equals word
chooseWhen: Pattern filtering with a single wildcard class
tradeoffs: A per-letter count table would be needed for the stricter rule
hack2hire:6a1cd98b8b879849ebc0fdaf.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: skeletons hiding one letter

clarifyingQuestions: Is the even-length median returned as a float or rounded?
May the input be reordered in place?
Is O(N) expected in the worst case or amortised?
hints: You only need one or two order statistics, not the whole sorted array.
Partition around a pivot and recurse only into the side holding the wanted rank.
Three-way partitioning keeps duplicate-heavy inputs linear; a fixed pseudo-random pivot sequence keeps both languages identical.
invariants: the wanted rank always lies in the current range
values left of the range are smaller and right of it are larger than any value inside
chooseWhen: One-off order statistics on large unsorted data
tradeoffs: Quickselect copies the input to avoid mutation; worst case is quadratic but needs adversarial pivots
hack2hire:68c2d9291f64f4312b0a3df2.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: linear-time median selection

clarifyingQuestions: What is the target of the operations: the reverse, a palindrome, something else?
Can a character be moved more than once?
Is the answer the count of moves or the moves themselves?
hints: Characters you never move stay in order and end up at the front.
So keep the longest prefix of the target that appears as a subsequence of image.
Every other character is moved once, in target order.
invariants: matched characters form a prefix of the target
the greedy earliest match maximises the matched prefix
chooseWhen: Minimum moves to the end to reach a permutation
tradeoffs: The greedy match is linear; recording the moves themselves needs O(n) more output
hack2hire:67a25626c5f86173882e3d8f.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: move-to-end operations to reach the reverse

clarifyingQuestions: Which games does a score threshold select: at or above, or below?
Must the threshold be one of the observed scores?
What is returned when no threshold qualifies?
How are proportions compared (exactly or as floats)?
hints: Group the games by score first.
Walking the distinct scores from high to low, the selected set only grows: keep running loss and total counts.
Check every prefix and keep the smallest qualifying score.
invariants: running counts equal the games with score >= the current score
scores are visited in decreasing order
chooseWhen: Tail statistics over a sorted key
tradeoffs: A hash map plus a sort of distinct scores beats rescanning per candidate
hack2hire:68ae7b5ec8631a6568126dbe.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: smallest score whose upper tail is loss-heavy enough

clarifyingQuestions: Is the goal to reach arr exactly with the fewest moves?
May values be negative?
Can the answer exceed 32-bit range?
hints: A move that covers a position can be extended rightwards for free while values do not drop.
New moves must start only where the value rises.
Sum the positive rises from left to right.
invariants: moves started so far equal the sum of rises up to i
every position is covered by exactly arr[i] moves
tradeoffs: The rise sum is the closed form of the divide-and-conquer recursion
hack2hire:678e72f4fa7ce9616e190fbc.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: fewest range increments

clarifyingQuestions: What are the trees of order 0 and 1?
How are nodes labelled?
Which step letters are used?
How large can n be?
hints: The tree is exponential in n, so never build it.
A subtree of order m has S(m) = 1 + S(m - 2) + S(m - 1) nodes; with pre-order labels, comparing a label with S(m - 2) tells you whether to go left or right.
Walk both labels from the root, drop the shared prefix, then go up once per remaining start step and follow the rest of the dest path.
invariants: the remaining label is always below the current subtree size
the common prefix ends at the lowest common ancestor
tradeoffs: Sizes up to order 75 fit exactly in a double; larger orders would need big integers
hack2hire:685303fe1af0034b3227652e.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: directions inside an implicit Fibonacci tree

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned when node n is unreachable within k edges?
Are self-loops or parallel edges present?
Is k a limit on edges or on intermediate nodes?
hints: If a bottleneck b is achievable, every larger b is too: the answer is monotone.
For a fixed b, keep only edges with weight <= b and ask whether the fewest-edge path to n has at most k edges.
Binary-search b over the distinct edge weights, testing each with a breadth-first search.
invariants: feasibility is monotone in the weight bound
breadth-first search gives the fewest-edge distance
chooseWhen: Bottleneck objectives combined with a hop limit
tradeoffs: Dijkstra on (bottleneck, hops) pairs fails because the two criteria conflict; binary search keeps it simple
hack2hire:68a5e98e3a368733bb10422e.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: hop-limited minimum bottleneck path

clarifyingQuestions: Must the pattern match the whole word or a substring?
Can "." match zero characters?
In which order should matches be returned?
hints: Treat each word separately: does the whole pattern match the whole word?
dp[i][j] says whether the first i characters of the word match the first j pattern symbols.
For "." either it consumes its first character (dp[i-1][j-1]) or it extends (dp[i-1][j]); keep only one row.
invariants: dp[0][0] is true and dp[0][j] is false for j > 0 because every symbol consumes a character
each row depends only on the previous row
tradeoffs: A trie walk could share prefixes, at the cost of more code
hack2hire:6a1f3ca28b879849ebc10ffb.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: wildcard filtering with one-or-more dots

clarifyingQuestions: Must the subset be non-empty?
Are the elements bounded by 2**31?
Is the size or the subset returned?
hints: When is an AND greater than zero?
Some single bit must be set in every chosen element.
For each bit count the elements that have it; the best bit gives the answer.
invariants: a subset with positive AND lies inside one bit's group
every bit group is itself a valid subset
chooseWhen: Bitwise subset questions with a common-bit structure
tradeoffs: Thirty counters replace an exponential search
hack2hire:69e51800ad1522fdaff14d5f.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: largest subset sharing a bit

clarifyingQuestions: Where does the cursor start?
Which letters denote moves and the key press?
If several shortest paths exist, which one is expected?
hints: Each letter c sits at row (c - a) // 5 and column (c - a) % 5.
Only z is dangerous: going down into row 5 must happen after moving left, and leaving z must go up first.
Emitting up and left moves before down and right moves satisfies both.
invariants: the cursor never leaves an occupied cell
each letter costs |dr| + |dc| moves plus one press
tradeoffs: A fixed move order makes the path unique; any other shortest order would be equally short
hack2hire:6795a8a1010c9ed2f849b1fd.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: alphabet-board key path

constraints: next only when hasNext is true
clarifyingQuestions: What does remove do when nothing was returned yet or it was already removed?
Does getVector keep rows that became empty?
Is next ever called past the end?
Must the original vector be left untouched?
hints: Copy the rows so the caller's vector never changes.
Keep a cursor (row, column) that is advanced past empty rows lazily in hasNext.
Do not shift arrays on remove: mark the last returned position as removed and rebuild rows only when a snapshot is requested.
invariants: the cursor always points at the next unreturned element or the end
a position can be removed at most once
chooseWhen: Iterators that must support deletion without invalidating the cursor
tradeoffs: Lazy deletion keeps remove O(1) but makes each snapshot O(total)
hack2hire:68dd9212fb98b196fa540558.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: 2D iterator with remove-last and snapshot

clarifyingQuestions: Is the distance Manhattan or Euclidean?
Must the lowest price and the fastest time come from the same restaurant?
What is returned when no restaurant offers the item?
Can the menu change after construction?
hints: The lowest price does not depend on the user: precompute it per item.
The fastest time does depend on the user: keep each item's list of restaurant locations.
A query is then one lookup plus one scan of that list.
invariants: each item index lists exactly the restaurants that offer it
delivery times are exact integers
chooseWhen: Many queries over a static catalogue
tradeoffs: A spatial index would beat the per-item scan for very large catalogues
hack2hire:68799c22ef2889afac734164.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: cheapest price and fastest delivery for one item

clarifyingQuestions: Is the distance Manhattan or Euclidean?
Must the lowest price and the fastest time come from the same restaurant?
What is returned when no restaurant offers the item?
Can the menu change after construction?
Can an order be split across restaurants?
hints: Level 1 stays as before: price per item precomputed, distances scanned.
For an order, only restaurants that offer the rarest item can qualify.
Probe each candidate's price in the other items' maps; sum prices and track both minima.
invariants: a qualifying restaurant offers every ordered item
both minima range over the same qualifying set
chooseWhen: Catalogue queries that intersect several inverted lists
tradeoffs: Starting from the rarest list bounds the work by the smallest posting list
hack2hire:6879a663ef2889afac734167.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: whole orders served by one restaurant

clarifyingQuestions: Are lines justified or padded?
How are consecutive articles separated?
Can a word be longer than maxWidth?
Is an article a string or a list of words?
hints: Handle each article on its own.
A word fits on the current line when line length + 1 + word length <= maxWidth.
Collect line word slices and join them once; insert "" between articles.

no line could take the next word

clarifyingQuestions: Are customers with fewer than k movies grouped?
Is the last-k window a set (duplicates collapse) or a multiset?
Are single-member groups returned?
How are groups and members ordered?
hints: Only the last k entries of each history matter.
Two sets are equal exactly when their sorted distinct elements are equal: use that as a hash key.
Bucket customers by key in input order and keep buckets with two or more members.
invariants: a bucket holds customers with identical last-k sets
insertion order of buckets follows first members
tradeoffs: Sorting each window costs O(k log k); a multiset hash would be faster but not collision-free
hack2hire:68e2c59adab409e303d92947.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: friend groups from identical last-k sets

clarifyingQuestions: Are customers with fewer than k movies grouped?
Is the last-k window a set (duplicates collapse) or a multiset?
Are single-member groups returned?
How are groups and members ordered?
Should a customer's group change as soon as a new movie arrives?
hints: Each watch slides one customer's window: one movie enters and, after k entries, one leaves.
Keep counts so you know when a movie enters or leaves the distinct set; only then does the key change.
Move the customer between key buckets kept as sorted lists, and answer queries by copying the bucket without the caller.
invariants: a customer is in exactly one bucket once they have k watches
bucket lists stay sorted
chooseWhen: Streaming equality grouping with sliding windows
tradeoffs: Sorted bucket lists make queries cheap but cost O(group size) per move
